sources.title: Teaching Your Child to Be a Good Sport
sources.quote: Accept a loss and focus on what they can do to improve rather than getting upset or blaming others. ... After a competition, don't focus on who won or lost. Instead, try asking, "What did you do well during the game?" or "Was there something you wish you could have done better?" If your child feels that something could have gone better, offer to work on it together before the next game. ... Shake hands before and after the game. ... Kids learn how to be a good sport from the adults in their lives, especially their parents and coaches.
sources.supports: Accepting a loss and focusing on improving, asking what went well and what could be better instead of who won, working on it together before the next game, shaking hands, and that kids learn sportsmanship from the adults around them. A sports page applied to home games as general advice.

sources.title: My child with ADHD is a sore loser. How can I help?
sources.quote: During family games, focus on the actual play. Make it about having fun together as a family instead of winning or losing. Model losing in a positive way. Congratulate the winner and acknowledge that everyone played well but some people played a bit better and won. Try to be specific about what you liked in how everyone played. Kids who lose often forget that they may have played really well and helped the team. ... Empathize with the feelings your child has, while also giving a positive outlook. ... Set short-term goals for becoming better at something he likes.
sources.supports: Play for fun, model losing, congratulate the winner, be specific about what each player did well, empathise with the feeling, and short goals in something the child enjoys. The page answers a parent of a 7-year-old with ADHD and says the situation is quite common; used here as general advice for a child who struggles to lose.

sources.title: Teaching Your Child Self-Control
sources.quote: As kids enter school, they're better able to understand the idea of consequences and that they can choose good or bad behavior. It may help your child to imagine a stop sign that must be obeyed and think about a situation before responding. Encourage your child to walk away from a frustrating situation for a few minutes to cool off instead of having an outburst. Praise kids when they do walk away and cool off. ... praise your child for not losing control in frustrating or difficult situations by saying things like, "I like how you stayed calm" or "Good job keeping your cool."
sources.supports: School-age kids can picture a stop sign and think before they react, walk away for a few minutes to cool off, and be praised for staying calm.

sources.title: Teaching Your Child to Be a Good Sport
sources.quote: Accept a loss and focus on what they can do to improve rather than getting upset or blaming others. ... After a competition, don't focus on who won or lost. Instead, try asking, "What did you do well during the game?" or "Was there something you wish you could have done better?" If your child feels that something could have gone better, offer to work on it together before the next game. ... Shake hands before and after the game. ... Kids learn how to be a good sport from the adults in their lives, especially their parents and coaches.
sources.supports: Accepting a loss and focusing on improving, asking what went well and what could be better instead of who won, working on it together before the next game, shaking hands, and that kids learn sportsmanship from the adults around them. A sports page applied to home games as general advice.

sources.title: My child with ADHD is a sore loser. How can I help?
sources.quote: During family games, focus on the actual play. Make it about having fun together as a family instead of winning or losing. Model losing in a positive way. Congratulate the winner and acknowledge that everyone played well but some people played a bit better and won. Try to be specific about what you liked in how everyone played. Kids who lose often forget that they may have played really well and helped the team. ... Empathize with the feelings your child has, while also giving a positive outlook. ... Set short-term goals for becoming better at something he likes.
sources.supports: Play for fun, model losing, congratulate the winner, be specific about what each player did well, empathise with the feeling, and short goals in something the child enjoys. The page answers a parent of a 7-year-old with ADHD and says the situation is quite common; used here as general advice for a child who struggles to lose.

sources.title: Teaching Your Child Self-Control
sources.quote: As kids enter school, they're better able to understand the idea of consequences and that they can choose good or bad behavior. It may help your child to imagine a stop sign that must be obeyed and think about a situation before responding. Encourage your child to walk away from a frustrating situation for a few minutes to cool off instead of having an outburst. Praise kids when they do walk away and cool off. ... praise your child for not losing control in frustrating or difficult situations by saying things like, "I like how you stayed calm" or "Good job keeping your cool."
sources.supports: School-age kids can picture a stop sign and think before they react, walk away for a few minutes to cool off, and be praised for staying calm.

sources.title: Restraint collapse: Why kids fall apart after school
sources.quote: After-school restraint collapse can happen to any child. ... Kids face a lot of demands at school beyond academics. They may be able to keep their stress and emotions in check while they're at school with their teachers and peers. When kids get home, they lose that self-control and experience after-school restraint collapse. Usually, restraint collapse happens where kids feel safest. And that's often at home, with people who support and understand them. ... "The best way to manage afterschool outbursts is to plan for decompression time right when kids get home. You want to address hunger, tiredness, and the need to share or connect about their day before you make any demands like homework or chores." ... Provide hugs, blanket wraps, calming music, and quiet space ... A snack can help your child get back on an even keel. ... If your child is upset or moody, it's natural to ask about problems at school. But doing that immediately may actually cause your child to focus on the negatives. "Try talking about what was good or best today, or what was challenging" ... Raising your voice will only increase the emotions your child is struggling with. Show empathy and say, "I can see you're upset. Take some time to calm down and we'll talk about it." ... If your child's form of emotional release is crying, be there with open arms. ... Wait until your child is calm. Talk in a neutral way that won't stir up more emotions.

sources.title: Restraint collapse: Why kids fall apart after school
sources.quote: After-school restraint collapse can happen to any child. ... Kids face a lot of demands at school beyond academics. They may be able to keep their stress and emotions in check while they're at school with their teachers and peers. When kids get home, they lose that self-control and experience after-school restraint collapse. Usually, restraint collapse happens where kids feel safest. And that's often at home, with people who support and understand them. ... "The best way to manage afterschool outbursts is to plan for decompression time right when kids get home. You want to address hunger, tiredness, and the need to share or connect about their day before you make any demands like homework or chores." ... Provide hugs, blanket wraps, calming music, and quiet space ... A snack can help your child get back on an even keel. ... If your child is upset or moody, it's natural to ask about problems at school. But doing that immediately may actually cause your child to focus on the negatives. "Try talking about what was good or best today, or what was challenging" ... Raising your voice will only increase the emotions your child is struggling with. Show empathy and say, "I can see you're upset. Take some time to calm down and we'll talk about it." ... If your child's form of emotional release is crying, be there with open arms. ... Wait until your child is calm. Talk in a neutral way that won't stir up more emotions.
